content: Lycopene is a vivid red carotenoid pigment and a phytochemical predominantly found in tomatoes and other red fruits. It is the most abundant carotenoid in the human body and is recognized as one of the most potent carotenoid antioxidants. The name lycopene is derived from the tomato's species classification, Solanum lycopersicum (formerly Lycopersicon esculentum). Structure and Chemistry Lycopene is a terpene molecule composed of eight isoprene units. Its red color arises from the presence of numerous conjugated carbon double bonds. These double bonds lower the energy required for electrons to transition to higher energy states, enabling the molecule to absorb visible light at progressively longer wavelengths. Lycopene absorbs most of the visible spectrum, which is why it appears red. When lycopene undergoes oxidation, such as through reactions with bleaching agents or acids, the carbon double bonds are broken, fragmenting the molecule into smaller compounds, each containing a carbon-oxygen double bond. Although these C=O bonds are also chromophoric, the shorter molecules cannot absorb sufficient light to appear colorful. Similarly, reduction of lycopene, which saturates the double bonds by converting them into single bonds, diminishes its ability to absorb light. Dietary Sources Lycopene is abundant in fruits and vegetables such as tomatoes, watermelon, pink grapefruit, pink guava, papaya, gac, and rosehip. Unlike many other nutrients, such as vitamin C, which degrade during cooking, the processing of tomatoes increases the concentration of bioavailable lycopene. For instance, lycopene in tomato paste is four times more bioavailable than in fresh tomatoes. This is because lycopene is highly insoluble in water and tightly bound to vegetable fibers. Processed tomato products, such as pasteurized tomato juice, soup, sauce, and ketchup, contain the highest concentrations of bioavailable lycopene. Cooking and crushing tomatoes, as in canning, and serving them in oil-rich dishes like spaghetti sauce or pizza, significantly enhance the absorption of lycopene from the digestive tract into the bloodstream. Lycopene is fat-soluble, and the presence of oil facilitates its absorption. Production Lycopene can be extracted from vegetables and fruits, particularly tomatoes. Another source of lycopene is the fungus Blakeslea trispora. Nutritional Benefits Lycopene is the most effective carotenoid in quenching singlet oxygen, a reactive oxygen species. It is 100 times more efficient in this role than vitamin E, which itself is 125 times more effective than glutathione, a water-soluble antioxidant. Singlet oxygen, often generated during ultraviolet light exposure, is a major contributor to skin aging. Due to its antioxidant properties, lycopene has been studied for its potential health benefits. Early research suggested that lycopene consumption might improve conditions such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, osteoporosis, and even male infertility. However, more recent studies have cast doubt on these claims, finding no significant link between lycopene and cancer prevention. In fact, a related antioxidant, beta-carotene, has been associated with an increased incidence of prostate cancer. Food Coloring Lycopene is widely used as a food coloring agent due to its ubiquity. It is not water-soluble and readily stains porous materials, including most plastics. While fresh tomato stains can be removed from fabric relatively easily, lycopene diffuses into plastics, making it resistant to removal with hot water, soap, or detergent. Bleach can destroy lycopene, but plastics are particularly prone to staining if they are heated, scratched, oiled, or exposed to acids. Formulations Available Lycopene is commercially available in combination formulations with other carotenoids and antioxidants. It is marketed by various pharmaceutical companies under different brand names, such as LYC-O-RED, LYNET, and LYCORICH.
